title: Sphaeranthus africanus: How to Spot and Control It in Rice
metaTitle: Sphaeranthus africanus in Rice: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Sphaeranthus africanus is an upright weed with winged stems and round flower heads. Learn how to spot it in rainfed rice fields and stop it before it seeds.
excerpt: Sphaeranthus africanus is an upright broadleaf weed from the daisy family, with winged stems and small round flower heads. It grows in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. It has no listed local or English name, so this page uses its scientific name. Here you will learn how to spot it and how to control it in your palay.

heroImage.alt: Sphaeranthus africanus, a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Vengolis, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Sphaeranthus africanus belongs to the Asteraceae, the daisy or sunflower family. The PhilRice weed list gives it no local name and no English name, so most guides call it by its scientific name. It grows upright and branches out as it gets older. You will find it in rainfed lowland rice fields, where it comes up with the crop.

This weed is an annual. It sprouts, grows, flowers and dies within one season, and it spreads only by seed. Each round flower head holds a cluster of tiny flowers, and each one can make a seed. When those seeds drop, they stay in the soil and sprout with the next crop. So even a few missed plants can mean a weedier field next season.

Look for an upright plant with leafy wings running along its stems and branches. These wings make the stem look flat and broad. As a broadleaf, it has wide, flat leaves with netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The leaves are oval to oblong, wider near the tip, with finely toothed edges. At the top, it carries many small round heads packed with greenish white flowers.

items: Upright plants with broad, leafy wings running down the stems and branches.
Oval to oblong leaves, wider near the tip, with fine teeth along the edges.
Many small, round flower heads at the ends of the branches.
Tight clusters of greenish white flowers packed into each round head.

blocks.text:
Sphaeranthus africanus competes with your palay for light, water and fertilizer. It stands upright and branches out, so a thick stand can shade young rice between the rows. Rice suffers most early in the season, before its leaves close over the field.

As an annual that spreads only by seed, its biggest threat comes later. Plants that you miss will flower, and each round head can add seed to the soil. Its seeds can also mix with harvested palay and lower the quality of your grain. So the weeds you skip this season come back in larger numbers next season.

items: Pull or cut plants before the round flower heads open, since every head that matures adds seed to your field.
Weed early in the season, while the plants are small and easy to pull from the soil.
Clean your tools and bunds after weeding, and do not leave flowering plants in the field to drop seed.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Sphaeranthus africanus down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Sphaeranthus africanus Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Sphaeranthus africanus?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Sphaeranthus africanus

items.q: What is Sphaeranthus africanus commonly called?
items.a: It has no local or English name in the PhilRice weed list. Farmers and technicians usually call it by its scientific name, or simply Sphaeranthus. It belongs to the daisy family. When you describe it to others, mention the winged stems and the round greenish white flower heads, since these set it apart from other weeds.

items.q: How do I control this weed in my rice field?
items.a: Start with prevention. Prepare the land well, plant clean seed and keep the bunds free of flowering weeds. Keep water in the field when rain allows. Hand weed early, before the flower heads open. If you need a herbicide, choose one by weed group and the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does this weed keep coming back each season?
items.a: It spreads only by seed, and each round flower head can hold many of them. If even a few plants flower before you weed, they drop seed into the soil. Those seeds then sprout with your next crop. The fix is simple but takes steady work. Weed early, and never let it flower.
